title: SQL Injection leading to Authentication Bypass in Login Endpoint
analysis:
The login handler in `routes/login.ts` retrieves the user's `email` from `req.body.email` and directly concatenates/interpolates it into a raw SQL query string passed to `models.sequelize.query()`. There is no parameterization, input sanitization, or validation of the email parameter, allowing an attacker to perform SQL injection. This allows bypass of authentication (login as any user, e.g., the administrator) and potential database manipulation or information disclosure.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker can POST to /rest/user/login with the following JSON request body:
{
  "email": "admin@juice-sh.op'--",
  "password": "any"
}

This results in the query:
SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = 'admin@juice-sh.op'--' ...
The trailing double-dash comments out the password validation check, logging the attacker in as the administrator without knowing the password.

title: SQL Injection in Product Search Endpoint
analysis:
The search products endpoint in `routes/search.ts` retrieves the search query `q` from user-supplied URL query parameters, truncates it to 200 characters, and directly interpolates it into a raw SQL query string passed to `models.sequelize.query()`. Due to lack of parameterization, sanitization, or validation, an attacker can input SQL payload strings to perform SQL Injection (e.g., UNION-based injection to extract sensitive information or schema structures from the database).

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker can perform a GET request such as:
GET /rest/products/search?q=apple')) UNION SELECT 1,id,email,password,4,5,6,7,8,9 FROM Users--

This bypasses any intended constraint and extracts passwords and emails from the Users table.
snippet:
let criteria: any = req.query.q === 'undefined' ? '' : req.query.q ?? ''
    criteria = (criteria.length <= 200) ? criteria : criteria.substring(0, 200)
    models.sequelize.query(`SELECT * FROM Products WHERE ((name LIKE '%${criteria}%' OR description LIKE '%${criteria}%') AND deletedAt IS NULL) ORDER BY name`)

title: Open Redirect via Weak Allowlist Validation
analysis:
The redirect endpoint in `routes/redirect.ts` allows users to specify an arbitrary URL in the `to` query parameter. The validation function `security.isRedirectAllowed()` in `lib/insecurity.ts` checks if the URL contains (via `url.includes(allowedUrl)`) any of the domains in the `redirectAllowlist`. Because it uses `includes()` instead of parsing the host and validating it properly, any URL that has an allowlisted domain as part of its path or query parameter string will bypass validation, resulting in an open redirect.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker can direct a victim to:
GET /redirect?to=https://attacker.com/?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop

Since 'https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop' is in the allowlist, the `includes` check evaluates to true, and the server redirects the user to the malicious domain `https://attacker.com/`.

title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) / Broken Access Control in Basket Retrieval
analysis:
The basket retrieval endpoint in `routes/basket.ts` allows any authenticated user to fetch the contents of any shopping basket by specifying the basket ID in the request parameters (`/rest/basket/:id`). Although the request must be authenticated, the application fails to verify that the requested basket ID actually belongs to the authenticated user's session (`user.bid`). An attacker can enumerate basket IDs to disclose items, addresses, and order histories of other customers.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
1. Log in to the application as a normal user.
2. Obtain a valid JWT authorization token.
3. Fetch a different user's basket (e.g., ID 1 or 2) by sending an HTTP GET request:
GET /rest/basket/1
Headers:
Authorization: Bearer <attacker_jwt_token>

This returns the basket details of user 1, bypassing any authorization bounds.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in Profile Image URL Upload
analysis:
The profile image URL upload feature in `routes/profileImageUrlUpload.ts` allows authenticated users to specify an arbitrary URL for their profile image. The server then retrieves this image using the request library's `request.get(url)` method. Because there is absolutely no input validation or sanitization restricting the target IP address, domain, port, or protocol, an attacker can use this feature to launch SSRF attacks against internal hosts, cloud metadata services (like AWS IMDS or GCP Metadata), or scan internal network ports.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker logs in and issues a profile update request or uploads a profile image via URL:
POST /profile/image/url
Headers:
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: token=<attacker_jwt_token>

{
  "imageUrl": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
}

The server fetches the AWS metadata page and potentially saves it to the static assets directory, or leaks info back to the user or logs.

title: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection in Complaint XML Upload
analysis:
The XML complaint upload handler in `routes/fileUpload.ts` accepts user-supplied XML files and parses them using the `libxmljs2` library with XML external entity expansion enabled (`noent: true`). Since external entities are resolved without restrictions, an attacker can submit a malicious XML file referencing local files or external resources to perform XML External Entity (XXE) Injection, potentially disclosing arbitrary files from the server's filesystem or initiating internal HTTP requests.

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker uploads a file named `complaint.xml` containing the following payload:
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="ISO-8859-1"?>
<!DOCTYPE foo [
  <!ELEMENT foo ANY >
  <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd" >
]>
<foo>&xxe;</foo>
```
When parsed by the server, the `/etc/passwd` file content replaces the `&xxe;` entity and is returned to the user in the subsequent deprecation error message, leaking host secrets.

title: Zip Slip (Arbitrary File Write / Path Traversal) via Unrestricted ZIP Unpacking
analysis:
The zip file upload handler in `routes/fileUpload.ts` extracts `.zip` archive entries directly to the server's disk using entry path values (`entry.path`). Although the application checks if the absolute resolved path contains the project root (`absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.'))`), it fails to ensure that the file stays within the intended subdirectory (`uploads/complaints/`). An attacker can craft a ZIP archive containing relative path traversal components (e.g. `../../ftp/legal.md`) to overwrite files inside other folders (such as `ftp/` or even code under `routes/`), leading to arbitrary file write / path traversal (Zip Slip).

Conceptual Exploit Payload:
An attacker creates a ZIP archive where one of the entries is named `../../ftp/legal.md` or `../../server.ts`. When uploaded to the complaints upload endpoint, `path.resolve('uploads/complaints/' + '../../ftp/legal.md')` resolves to `<project_root>/ftp/legal.md`. The validation check `absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.'))` is bypassed because the target is still inside the workspace directory, allowing the attacker to overwrite the legal disclaimer file or other critical application files.
